title: I made a free ski and snowboard game on the mountains I ski (Mount Hood and Mt. Bachelor) with Claude Code (Opus 5.5, Extra effort)
author: See_Yourself_Now
selftext:
I've made a  game where you can ski or snowboard the real Oregon mountains (Mount Hood and Mt. Bachelor ski areas) in your browser. I've seen skiing and snowboarding games, but I wanted something I could relate to, and I thought it would be  cool to  be on the same runs and mountains I frequent.

It's as accurate as I could get with the resources at hand. The mountains come from USGS elevation data, and the runs, lifts and lodges come from OpenStreetMap. So, Timberline, Mount Hood Meadows, Skibowl and Bachelor are laid out the way they really are: runs, off-piste areas, lifts and all. You can free-ride from any lift, pick any run on the mountain, race the gates against par times or three AI riders, drop the cliffs in Heather Canyon, get caught in a storm, or ride Palmer in July.

**How I built it.** I directed and tested; Claude Code (Opus 5.5 extra effort in multiple long sessions) wrote about 18,000 lines of plain JavaScript and three.js, no game engine, over roughly three days of sessions. Nothing about the mountains is made up by the AI. A Python script pulls the USGS elevation (an 8 m grid), the OpenStreetMap data, and the Forest Service's canopy map for how thick the trees are. The AI was strongest at that data pipeline, the physics and the shaders, and at building its own test tools. It can't play the game, so it built a way to render real frames without a window, plus AI racers that ski the courses to check the physics after every change. For one review round I had a Claude Fable 5.1 play it through screenshots and  OpenAI Astra read the code. They caught completely different problems, including that trick scoring had never actually worked.

There was a lot of back and forth to get what I was looking for from years of actually skiing these places. It gets things plausible, but not right, until someone who skis there says "this double black feels like a blue" (the terrain was accurate; the camera made steep look flat), or "the gate for Jack's Woods starts on the traverse". Phone implementation also had challenges related to less graphical capability, and sound stopping when switching apps. 

I recommend playing on desktop if available but it plays on phones and tablets too. Hold your phone sideways and use the thumb stick, or tilt the phone to steer and flick it to jump (in the pause menu). Free, nothing to download: [https://lejup.studiozalktis.com/](https://lejup.studiozalktis.com/) (On a computer: keyboard or gamepad. The first load takes a few seconds while the mountain downloads.)

Happy to answer questions about the workflow, and I'd love feedback or additional thoughts.
